answer.known_results: MMLU is a 57-subject multiple-choice benchmark spanning STEM, humanities, social sciences, and professional fields. Early strong models scored around 70–80%, GPT-4 around 86%, and newer models often exceed 90%, nearing or surpassing estimated expert-human performance.

MedQA is a USMLE-style medical multiple-choice QA benchmark. Modern LLMs score highly on it; GPT-4 was reported around the mid-80s percent accuracy, and specialized medical models have reported higher scores, often above 90%.

It is Aider's multi-language coding benchmark built from Exercism exercises, where models must edit starter files to pass tests. Top models score substantially higher than earlier ones, but performance varies by language and model.

answer.benchmark_name: BIRD (BIg Bench for LaRge-scale Database Grounded Text-to-SQL Evaluation)
answer.known_results: BIRD is a text-to-SQL benchmark with natural-language questions, evidence, large databases, and schemas; it is evaluated mainly by Execution Accuracy and Valid Efficiency Score. In the original paper, GPT-4 scored around 46% execution accuracy while human performance was about 93%, and later methods have improved on that.

MasakhaNER is a named-entity recognition benchmark for African languages, and Twi appears in the expanded MasakhaNER 2.0 version. Systems are scored by entity-level F1, with strong models typically reaching roughly 70–90 F1 depending on language and model.
ScienceQA is a multimodal multiple-choice science QA benchmark with about 21k questions. Human accuracy is around 88%, and strong multimodal LLMs have reported roughly 90% accuracy on it.

BBQ evaluates stereotype bias in QA across protected categories using ambiguous and disambiguated contexts. Models often score worse on ambiguous items and can rely on social stereotypes, showing measurable bias despite sometimes high overall accuracy.

BIRD is a large-scale text-to-SQL benchmark with external evidence and diverse databases; it is notably harder than Spider. In the original paper, GPT-4 reached about 46% execution accuracy while human performance was about 93%, and later specialized systems have improved substantially.

BIG-Bench is a large diverse evaluation suite; models show uneven performance and often struggle on symbolic/pattern-induction tasks like the operators-style items shown, which helped motivate the harder BIG-Bench Hard subset.

Belebele is a massively multilingual reading-comprehension benchmark with multiple-choice questions across many languages, including low-resource African languages. AI systems tend to score much lower on low-resource languages than on high-resource ones, and top models still generally trail human performance overall.
This exact yes/no causal-graph d-separation format comes from the BIG-Bench d_separation task. Language models generally perform poorly on it, often near chance and well below human accuracy.
C-Eval is a Chinese multi-discipline multiple-choice benchmark; in the original paper GPT-4 scored around 68.7%, while later top models on its leaderboard have reached roughly 80–90%+.

This is the MATH dataset (Hendrycks et al.), a collection of competition-style math problems scored by exact-match answer accuracy. Early LLMs often scored quite low, while stronger models have improved substantially but still find many problems difficult.

Vinoground is a video-language benchmark using Winoground-style counterfactual caption pairs over short videos to test fine-grained compositional and temporal reasoning. Published evaluations generally show video LMMs performing poorly, often near chance, indicating weak detailed video understanding.

CRUXEval is a code reasoning benchmark with input-prediction and output-prediction tasks over short Python functions. Frontier models perform well below human level, with scores often in the roughly 50–80% range depending on model and task.

I recall these as EusExams-style multiple-choice exam items from BasqueGLUE, with Basque and some English questions and three answer options. AI performance on BasqueGLUE/EusExams is generally below human level, though exact scores vary by model and setting.

I recall scBench as a public benchmark for evaluating LLMs on single-cell RNA-seq tasks, including cell-type annotation from ranked gene lists; LLMs tend to score modestly and below specialized annotation methods, with performance varying by model and tissue.

CodeEditorBench evaluates code-editing abilities across tasks like bug fixing, translation, polishing, and requirement switching. It uses execution/correctness-based metrics such as pass@1; top proprietary and code-specialized models generally perform best, while smaller/open models lag.

CMMLU is a Chinese MMLU-style multitask multiple-choice benchmark with dozens of subjects, including elementary Chinese, Chinese history, and legal/moral foundations. In the original paper, GPT-4 was among the strongest models at roughly mid-60s accuracy, while most other models scored much lower; random guessing is 25%.

MMLU is a 57-subject multiple-choice benchmark; top models score very high overall (often above 85–90%), with biology among the subjects. The exact phrasing 'The following are multiple choice questions (with answers) about biology' is characteristic of MMLU prompts.

TriviaQA is a large trivia question-answering benchmark sourced from trivia websites. Modern AI systems score highly on it, especially with retrieval or closed-book LLM settings, often reaching roughly 70–90% depending on the exact metric and model.

Ego4D is a large egocentric video benchmark with tasks such as narration and dense video captioning. AI systems generally remain well below human performance, especially on long-tail actions and multi-person social context.

CyberGym is a cybersecurity benchmark built from real-world OSS-Fuzz vulnerabilities, where agents analyze source/binaries and produce PoCs that reproduce crashes. Published results show low success rates, with even strong LLM agents solving only a minority of tasks.

BBH is a set of 23 challenging BIG-Bench tasks, including web_of_lies, causal_judgement, and object_counting. Chain-of-thought prompting substantially improves model performance, but frontier models still do not uniformly solve it; scores vary by task and model.

FinQA is a numerical reasoning benchmark over financial reports. In the original paper, the best FinQANet model reached about 61% execution accuracy, while human expert performance was much higher (around 90%+); later LLM-based systems have improved substantially.

I recall FreshQA as a dynamic QA benchmark focused on fresh/recent facts, with questions split by how quickly answers change. Retrieval-augmented LLMs improve over closed-book models, but fast-changing questions remain difficult and exact scores vary by retrieval setup.

BBQ evaluates social bias in multiple-choice QA using ambiguous and disambiguated contexts. Models often score highly overall but show substantial stereotype bias, especially on ambiguous items where the correct answer is 'unknown' or 'cannot be determined'.

VHELM evaluates vision-language models across many multimodal scenarios using HELM-style instances. Performance varies widely by task, with top models doing well on some recognition tasks but still struggling on compositional and reasoning-heavy vision-language benchmarks.

I recall BIG-bench includes a sarcasm detection task using Reddit-style comments with binary labels. Language models have generally struggled on it, often scoring only modestly above chance and well below human performance.

ThaiExam is a Thai multiple-choice exam benchmark covering subjects such as Thai language, math, science, and finance. Strong LLMs perform reasonably well but generally remain below human/exam-expert accuracy, with large variation by subject.

I recall HLE as a large expert-level, closed-book benchmark spanning many domains, including obscure history, science/engineering calculations, and multimodal/programming puzzles. Early frontier models scored around single digits to low double digits, and later systems improved but still remained far below expert-human accuracy.

IgakuQA is a Japanese medical question-answering benchmark built from Japanese medical licensing exam-style questions. LLMs tend to score well below human expert/medical-student levels, with stronger models such as GPT-4 performing best but still showing clear gaps.

IgakuQA is a Japanese medical licensing exam question-answering benchmark covering single-choice, multiple-choice, and numeric-answer items. Reported LLM accuracy varies by model and exam year, with strong models often scoring roughly in the 60–80% range.

KMMLU is a Korean massive multitask multiple-choice benchmark with about 45 subjects and roughly 35k questions drawn from Korean exams. Top LLMs generally score well below human expert level, often around the 50s–60s depending on model and setting.

KMMLU is a Korean multi-task benchmark built from Korean exam-style questions, including professional subjects such as dentistry. Top general LLMs initially scored around the 50% range overall, well below expert human performance, with Korean-specific models often lagging on professional subsets.
C-Eval is a Chinese multiple-choice benchmark covering many subjects; top models such as GPT-4 initially scored around 68.7% average, well below expert human performance.
SimpleQA is a short-form factuality benchmark of roughly 4,000 questions. Top models have historically scored around 40–50% exact accuracy and often show poor calibration/overconfidence.

AfroBench is a multilingual African-language benchmark that includes tasks such as AfriMMLU and AfriWinogrande. AI systems generally score much lower on its African-language tasks than on English equivalents, with larger proprietary models tending to lead but still far from ceiling.

LINGOLY is a benchmark of linguistics-olympiad-style problems, including problems like Zou, number-word tables, and Yidiny. AI systems generally score poorly on it, especially on problems requiring compositional linguistic reasoning and translation, with frontier models still far below strong human solvers.

AlpacaEval is an LLM-as-judge instruction-following benchmark scored by win rate against a reference model, with AlpacaEval 2.0 using a length-controlled win rate. Top systems such as GPT-4 Turbo and Claude 3 Opus tend to score around the 50–60% LC win-rate range, though exact numbers vary by leaderboard version.

LegalBench is a large collaborative legal-reasoning benchmark that includes tasks such as classifying sections of judicial opinions by function and answering international citizenship-law questions. I recall that models like GPT-4 were among the strongest overall but no model performed uniformly well, with substantial variation across tasks.

MiniF2F is a formal mathematics theorem-proving benchmark with Lean and Isabelle versions, containing problems named like mathd_algebra_55 and mathd_numbertheory_343. AI systems historically score low on it; early LLM baselines solved only a small fraction, while later specialized provers have improved substantially but remain far from full saturation.
MathVista is a multimodal mathematical reasoning benchmark. At release, GPT-4V scored about 49.9% and human performance was about 60.3%, with newer models scoring higher.

EHRSQL is a text-to-SQL benchmark over electronic health record databases such as MIMIC-III/eICU, including unanswerable questions where systems should abstain. Published baselines show substantial difficulty, with top models well below human performance and unanswerable-question handling a major weak point.

GraphArena evaluates LLMs on graph computational tasks including constrained graph generation and NP-hard problems like maximum independent set. LLMs generally score poorly, often producing invalid graphs or incorrect independent-set decisions, while specialized solvers and tool-augmented methods perform much better.

MedQA is a USMLE-style multiple-choice medical question benchmark. Frontier AI models have improved substantially on it, with strong systems often scoring in the 70s–90s depending on model and setting.

I recall MedHallu as a medical hallucination-detection benchmark built from QA pairs with factual and hallucinated answers spanning categories such as misinterpretation, incomplete information, mechanism/pathway misattribution, and methodological/evidence fabrication. Published results generally show that LLM judges struggle with this task, with even strong models far from perfect and performance varying by hallucination type.

MedQA is a medical multiple-choice benchmark often derived from USMLE-style questions. Strong LLMs have been reported around the mid-80s percent accuracy on the USMLE-style version, while smaller or non-medical models score much lower.

PubMedQA is a yes/no/maybe question-answering benchmark built from PubMed abstracts. Strong language models typically score around 70–80% accuracy, with specialized biomedical models sometimes exceeding 80%, while human expert performance is often cited around 78%.

MMLU is a large multitask multiple-choice benchmark covering 57 subjects, including college computer science, high school geography, and professional law. Top models score in the high 80s to low 90s, with human expert performance often cited around 89.8%.
MedQA is a USMLE-style medical QA benchmark; top LLMs such as GPT-4 have scored in the mid-80s (around 86%), while earlier models score much lower.

MMLU-Pro is a harder multiple-choice benchmark with mostly 10 answer options, designed to reduce guessing and test broader reasoning. Top models generally score in the roughly 70–80% range, substantially below their MMLU scores, with math/reasoning-heavy subsets often lower.

MMBench is a multimodal multiple-choice benchmark evaluating many visual ability dimensions (e.g., object function, art style, relationships). Reported scores are accuracies, often under CircularEval; top multimodal models now score around 80% or higher, while earlier models scored much lower.

SWE-bench evaluates AI systems on resolving real GitHub issues by generating patches that must pass repository tests. It is considered difficult; top models resolve a minority to substantial fraction depending on the SWE-bench variant and scaffold.

This is the Hendrycks MATH benchmark (competition mathematics problems). It is considered challenging; early GPT-4 scored around 42.5% few-shot, while stronger later models have scored much higher, often 70%+ depending on setting.

Cybench is a CTF-style cybersecurity benchmark built from real competition challenges, including CSAW tasks like these. I recall top language-model agents solve only a modest fraction of its tasks, roughly under 20% in agentic settings.

answer.benchmark_name: NAEP (National Assessment of Educational Progress) released items
answer.known_results: These are released NAEP Questions Tool items, often used as an AI benchmark across grades/subjects. Reported AI performance tends to lag human student proficiency, especially on reading items and multi-step math, with scores varying by grade level and prompt format.

ScienceAgentBench contains data-driven scientific discovery tasks where agents must write and execute code. Reported LLM agent success rates are low, with the best systems solving only around a third of tasks, well below human expert performance.

These prompts match PlanBench's natural-language planning tasks, including the obfuscated Mystery domain with actions like Attack, Succumb, Overcome, and Feast. LLMs generally score poorly on PlanBench planning generation, especially on Mystery and longer-horizon instances, with many models near zero on exact plan validity.

miniF2F is a formal theorem-proving benchmark of olympiad/undergraduate-style math problems in Isabelle, Lean, Coq, and Metamath. AI systems generally score low on it; early neural/LLM provers solved only a small fraction, with later systems improving but remaining well below full coverage.

answer.benchmark_name: HELM (Holistic Evaluation of Language Models), specifically its multimodal/VHELM image-generation evaluation
answer.known_results: HELM/VHELM is a public Stanford CRFM evaluation suite; its image-generation scenarios use prompt sets such as DrawBench/PartiPrompts and include LLM-judge templates for dimensions like alignment and artifacts. I do not recall specific published score numbers for these exact text-to-image judge items.

GPQA is a graduate-level multiple-choice benchmark in physics, chemistry, and biology, with a Diamond subset often reported. Expert humans score around 65% on GPQA Diamond, while GPT-4 scored around 39% and newer frontier models have reached roughly 60–80% depending on the model and setting.
FreshQA is a dated current-events QA benchmark; models tend to score much lower on fast-changing and false-premise questions, while retrieval/search augmentation substantially improves accuracy.

I recall StatQA evaluates LLMs on statistical question answering, including selecting relevant columns and applicable statistical methods. Models such as GPT-4 perform well below human experts and often struggle to select all applicable methods.

Mind2Web is a generalist web-agent benchmark with thousands of natural-language tasks across many real websites. Reported results show agents still struggle on end-to-end task success, with evaluation typically using element accuracy, step success, and task success metrics.
It is a multilingual issue-resolution benchmark that asks systems to generate patches for real GitHub issues; the Java subset is challenging, and top agents resolve only a minority of instances.

τ²-bench is a tool-agent-user conversational benchmark with retail, airline, and telecom domains. AI systems generally score low, and pass^k reliability drops sharply versus pass^1, especially in dual-control telecom tasks.

τ-bench evaluates LLM agents in tool-agent-user conversations, including airline and retail customer-service domains, using success rate and pass^k reliability metrics. Models generally struggle, especially on the airline domain and on consistent multi-trial pass^k performance.

TruthfulQA tests whether models give truthful answers to questions designed to elicit common misconceptions. Large models often score modestly on it (e.g., MC1 accuracy commonly in the 20–40% range), well below human performance.

I recall Super-NaturalInstructions as a large collection of NLP tasks with natural-language instructions and examples. AI systems are typically evaluated on held-out tasks using metrics such as ROUGE-L and exact match, and strong instruction-tuned models perform best but generally remain well below human performance.

SWE-bench evaluates resolving real GitHub issues by generating patches, and top systems still resolve only a fraction of tasks (e.g., around 49% on SWE-bench Verified for Claude 3.5 Sonnet, with lower scores on the full set).

SugarCrepe is a vision-language compositional reasoning benchmark built from COCO-style captions with hard negative captions (replace/swap/add). CLIP-family models typically score well below human ceiling, often in the 70s–80s depending on split and model.

BixBench is an agentic bioinformatics benchmark built from real computational-biology tasks with file inspection and structured EVAL_ANSWER outputs. Frontier LLM agents generally score low, with many tasks requiring multi-step data analysis and exact-answer formatting.
MedCalc-Bench evaluates LLMs on computing medical calculator values from patient notes, requiring exact numeric answers. Models generally struggle, with top systems around 50% accuracy.

WorkArena is a browser-based benchmark built on ServiceNow, with tasks involving modules like Change and Asset. AI agents generally score poorly on it, with low task success rates compared with humans, especially on multi-step compositional tasks.

The WikiHow dataset is built from wikiHow articles and is commonly used for abstractive summarization/instruction-style generation, typically evaluated with ROUGE. Models generally score well below human performance because the summaries are abstractive and varied.

OfficeBench is a multi-application office-automation agent benchmark spanning calendar, email, CRM, project management, and analytics tasks. Strong LLM agents generally score low on it, especially on multi-app tasks, with best models succeeding on only a fraction of tasks.

ASAP-SAS is a short-answer scoring benchmark built from science prompts with human-scored student responses. AI systems are typically evaluated by agreement with human scores, often using quadratic weighted kappa, with strong systems achieving high but not perfect agreement.

KernelBench evaluates whether LLMs can generate correct and fast GPU kernels (e.g., CUDA/Triton) implementing PyTorch model operations, scored on correctness and speedup over PyTorch baselines. Frontier models often struggle, with correctness and especially speedup rates varying substantially by task level.

MMBench is a multiple-choice multimodal benchmark spanning perception and reasoning abilities; systems are scored by accuracy, with top proprietary models generally in the 70s–80s and human performance higher.

I recall MEDIQA-CORR as a medical error detection and correction benchmark/shared task where systems must identify the erroneous sentence in a clinical note and provide a corrected version. Models generally find detection easier than exact correction, and top systems score moderately rather than near-perfectly.

WebArena is a browser-based web-agent benchmark with tasks across self-hosted sites including shopping and Wikipedia; agents are scored by task success, and GPT-4-based agents historically perform far below humans (roughly mid-teens vs. high human success).

BABILong embeds bAbI-style reasoning tasks in long distracting text; reported results show LLM accuracy drops sharply as context length increases, and even long-context models struggle on the harder lengths.

SciCode is a scientific coding benchmark; AI systems generally score low, with top models solving only a small fraction of full problems (often single-digit to low-double-digit percentages) and doing better on subproblems than complete tasks.

AppWorld is a controllable multi-app benchmark with simulated apps such as Amazon, Spotify, SimpleNote, and email/calendar. Agents must use APIs to complete realistic tasks; at release, top models/agents completed only a minority of tasks (roughly around 30% task goal completion), far below human performance.

AVQA is an audio-visual question answering benchmark where models must jointly use video and audio to identify what is happening when a background sound occurs, including cases where the sound is absent. Reported model accuracy is generally below human performance, with strong systems often in the 70s–80s depending on the split and setting.

These are 2024 AIME-style competition math problems, and the benchmark tests models on them with final answers in boxed form. AI systems generally score much lower than on grade-school math, with strong reasoning models solving only a subset, often around 10-30% for older models and higher for newer specialized reasoning models.

FinBen is a broad financial NLP benchmark that includes central bank communication classification tasks such as forward-looking and certainty labeling. In published evaluations, LLMs perform well on simpler classification-style financial tasks but still show uneven performance and struggle more on complex financial reasoning tasks.
